title: Ditch to Intake
subtitle: Prairie Line River Crossing Release & Water Intakes

brief.userPrompt: Tuesday 8 June 2027, clear and warm, the Kansas River at about 8,500 cfs with a surface velocity near 2.3 miles per hour (2 knots). The exercise starts at 05:45 in the Ironbark Pipeline Control Center in Tulsa (shift supervisor Nadia Kowalczyk). At 05:52 the Prairie Line shows a 46 psi pressure drop in 2 minutes and a 1.8 percent flow imbalance at the Prairie Bend segment (milepost 214.3, Kansas River crossing); at 06:02 a leak cannot be ruled out, at 06:04 the line is shut down and at 06:09 block valves at Mill Ridge Station (milepost 213.1) and Sandhill Valve (milepost 215.6) are closed. Volume balance suggests 2,700 to 3,500 barrels of medium sour crude released (the medium case of 3,100 is the planning figure; the worst case is 8,400 barrels). Crude reaches the river through a drainage ditch at about 06:40, first reported by a fisherman to the county 911 before Ironbark's own report to the National Response Center. Pressure points: the shift supervisor as person in charge calls the NRC without waiting for the Qualified Individual (Director of Operations Teresa Holloway), then the QI calls the OSRO (Prairie Spill Response Cooperative, Duty Manager Alicia Brandt, first boom at the nearest ramp 3.5 hours after notification), the Kansas Department of Health and Environment, county emergency management and the water intakes in the plan's order; a notification to a utility's general line must not count until the operator is reached; Ironbark estimates are given as ranges with their basis and in barrels only; EPA Region 7 is the Federal On-Scene Coordinator and forms a Unified Command with the state; the Incident Management Team activates at Level 2 for a release over 1,000 barrels with Gordon Iwata as Incident Commander and Cole Whitfield in the Environmental Unit; the trajectory gives windows (the Prairie Bend Rural Water District intake at mile 11 serving 6,200 customers in about 4.8 hours, nesting piping plover sandbars at miles 6 to 9, the Cottonwood Slough mussel bed at mile 22, the Sterling Bluff Water Department intake at mile 34 serving 41,000 people in about 14.8 hours); the river current is 2 knots so boom must be angled to deflect rather than set square; the cooperative has 9,500 feet of river boom across its depots and limited boats; the Prairie Bend Rural Water District has no wells and 1.1 million gallons of storage and must decide whether to close its intake and buy from Sterling Bluff; the Sterling Bluff Director (Odell Prescott) has about 34 hours of supply without the river and must close the intake himself, with the closure complete an hour before the earliest arrival; a request for in-situ burning or dispersant would not be preauthorized on the Kansas River and only the FOSC can authorize it; the Joint Information Center must use one volume figure and never say that the water is safe; a claims line opens; wildlife and the US Fish and Wildlife Service direct work near the sandbars; recreational fishing and the Mill Ridge ramp are closed by the state. Decisions the exercise should record: notifications with who and time, OSRO activation and equipment, protection priorities and strategy, boom deployed with the time it will be in place against arrival, the water intake closure, fishery or shoreline closure, countermeasure request, escalation of the IMT, public statements. Produce a PREP exercise record at the end (core components exercised, not a worst case discharge). The SimCell plays the National Response Center, EPA Region 7, the Kansas Department of Health and Environment, the Kansas Department of Wildlife and Parks, the US Fish and Wildlife Service, county emergency management, the Prairie Bend Rural Water District manager, PHMSA, reporters and residents.

overview.theme: Who calls whom, and when; one consistent volume range; protecting the river and the water intakes against the time oil takes to arrive; and making clear who decides what, since closures and countermeasures are not Ironbark's decisions.
overview.threat: On Tuesday 8 June 2027 the Prairie Line fails at the Prairie Bend segment Kansas River crossing (milepost 214.3). There is no attacker, and the cause is unknown and must not be guessed. At 05:52 the Ironbark Pipeline Control Center in Tulsa sees a 46 psi pressure drop in 2 minutes and a 1.8 percent flow imbalance. At 06:02 a leak cannot be ruled out. The line is shut down at 06:04, and the block valves at Mill Ridge Station (milepost 213.1) and Sandhill Valve (milepost 215.6) are closed by 06:09. The SCADA volume balance puts the release at 2,700 to 3,500 barrels of medium sour crude, with 3,100 barrels as the planning figure. This is an estimate, not confirmed, and it is not a worst case discharge. At about 06:40 the crude reaches the Kansas River through a drainage ditch. The river is running about 8,500 cfs at about 2 knots and carries the oil toward the Mill Ridge boat ramp, the piping plover nesting sandbars at miles 6 to 9, the Prairie Bend Rural Water District intake at mile 11, the Cottonwood Slough mussel bed at mile 22 and the Sterling Bluff Water Department intake at mile 34.
overview.operationalImpact: Shift supervisor Nadia Kowalczyk has a shut-in line with an unconfirmed loss. As person in charge, the supervisor has to report to the National Response Center within 15 minutes without waiting for the Qualified Individual. Meanwhile a fisherman has already called county 911, so the county, reporters and residents hear about the spill before Ironbark's report. QI Teresa Holloway has to activate Prairie Spill Response Cooperative, whose Duty Manager Alicia Brandt reports that the first boom can be at the nearest ramp about 3.5 hours after notification. The cooperative has 9,500 feet of river boom spread across its depots and only a few boats. At a 2-knot current the boom must be angled to deflect oil, not set square across the flow. The QI also has to reach KDHE, county emergency management and the intake operators in the plan's order. A call to a utility's general line does not count until the operator is reached. The IMT escalates to Level 2, with Gordon Iwata as Incident Commander and Cole Whitfield leading the Environmental Unit, and forms a Unified Command with the FOSC from EPA Region 7 and the KDHE state OSC at Mill Ridge Station. The trajectory, given as time windows with the model run time, shows oil at the rural water district intake in about 4.8 hours. The district has no wells and only storage, so its manager must decide whether to close the intake and buy water from Sterling Bluff. Oil reaches the Sterling Bluff intake in about 14.8 hours. Director Odell Prescott has about 34 hours of supply without the river and must close the intake himself, with closure finished an hour before the earliest arrival. Sterling Bluff also has to call the dialysis center, the medical center and the nursing homes directly. USFWS directs any work near the nesting sandbars. The state closes recreational fishing and the Mill Ridge ramp. Any request for in-situ burning or dispersant goes to the FOSC because it is not preauthorized on this river. The JIC has to issue one volume range, never say the water is safe, and open a claims line while phones fill with calls from the press, residents and fishers.

objectives.name: Notification and Activation
objectives.text: Demonstrate the ability to make the National Response Center report within 15 minutes of the 06:02 'leak cannot be ruled out' decision, then reach the QI, KDHE, county emergency management, Prairie Spill Response Cooperative and the intake operators (not general lines) in the order set by the Ironbark Response Plan, and log each contact with its time.

objectives.name: Technical Analysis
objectives.text: Demonstrate the ability to produce and update a river trajectory, with arrival windows and the model run time, for the Mill Ridge ramp, the plover sandbars at miles 6 to 9, the mile 11 rural water district intake, Cottonwood Slough and the mile 34 Sterling Bluff intake, and to use it to rank protection priorities on the ICS 232.

objectives.name: Decision Making
objectives.text: Demonstrate the ability to decide where to put 9,500 feet of river boom and the few available boats in a 2-knot current, using angled deflection booming that is in place before landfall and keeping clear of the plover nests until USFWS is consulted, and to route any burn or dispersant request to the FOSC because neither is preauthorized on this river.

objectives.name: Communication and Authority
objectives.text: Demonstrate the ability to issue Joint Information Center messages, cleared by Ironbark, EPA, KDHE and county PIOs, that use one barrel range with its SCADA basis, leave intake closures and drinking water status to the utilities and the state, and open a claims line while the county 911 call has the story out first.

roles.name: Qualified Individual / Incident Commander (Ironbark)
roles.team: Team A: Qualified Individual / Incident Commander (Ironbark)
roles.description: Owns plan activation, the IMT activation level, funding commitments up to $5 million, the OSRO contract and Ironbark's seat in the Unified Command at Mill Ridge Station.
standingOrders: Activate: any release to water over 1,000 barrels means a Level 2 IMT now, not after the volume is confirmed.
Commit: put money and the OSRO in motion right away; arguing over cost in the first hours costs river miles.
Lane: Ironbark pays and proposes; it does not close intakes, fisheries or ramps, and it does not authorize burning or dispersant.
Unify: bring objectives to the Unified Command for the ICS 202 instead of acting alone, even when the FOSC or state OSC is slower than you would like.

roles.name: Control Center Shift Supervisor
roles.team: Team B: Control Center Shift Supervisor
roles.description: Owns line shutdown, valve isolation, SCADA and computational pipeline monitoring data, and the first report as the person in charge.
standingOrders: Shut Down: if a leak cannot be ruled out, stop the line and close the block valves; restarting to test it is not an option.
Report: call the National Response Center within 15 minutes as the person in charge; do not wait for the QI to approve the call.
Estimate: give the volume as a barrel range with its SCADA volume-balance basis, and never say what caused the failure.
Record: write down every alarm, valve time and call as it happens, because the incident file goes to the regulatory investigation.

roles.name: Environmental Unit Leader
roles.description: Owns the trajectory, the ICS 232 Resources at Risk ranking, the sampling plan and the coordination needed with the trustee agencies.
standingOrders: Windows: give every arrival estimate as an earliest-to-latest window with the model run time, and rerun it when river flow or observations change.
Rank: protect the drinking water intakes first, then the listed species and the mussel bed, and show the reasoning on the ICS 232.
Consult: keep crews off the piping plover sandbars until USFWS has directed the work, even if that leaves the boom short.
Evidence: recommend reopening an intake only on test results, never because a deadline is pushing you.

roles.name: Public Information Officer (Joint Information Center)
roles.team: Team D: Public Information Officer / Joint Information Center
roles.description: Owns Ironbark's messages through the Joint Information Center, the media and resident inquiries, and the claims line.
standingOrders: Clear: release nothing until the JIC has cleared it, even while the 911-driven news coverage gets ahead of you.
One Number: use only the single barrel range and its basis that the JIC has agreed on; do not round it to sound smaller.
Truth over Reassurance: never say the water is safe to drink; refer drinking water questions to the utilities and the state.
Claims: announce the claims line early and send fishers and residents to it.

roles.name: OSRO Duty Manager (Prairie Spill Response Cooperative)
roles.team: Team E: OSRO Duty Manager (Prairie Spill Response Cooperative)
roles.description: Manages the cooperative's responders, boats, vacuum trucks and river boom from the Topeka, Wichita and Kansas City sites against the Tier 1 and Tier 2 commitments.
standingOrders: Real ETAs: report real arrival times for crews and boom, even when they miss what the IMT hopes for.
Angle: at about 2 knots, deflect boom toward collection points; never set it square across the current.
Allocate: put scarce boom where the Unified Command's priorities say, not wherever the first caller asks.
Escalate: call in Tier 2 and subcontractors early so you are not waiting for the shortfall to show.

roles.name: Director (Sterling Bluff Water Department)
roles.team: Team F: Water Department Director (Sterling Bluff)
roles.description: Owns the decisions to close and reopen the Sterling Bluff intake, supply management for 41,000 customers, and direct notice to critical-care customers.
standingOrders: Close Early: have the gate closed and the line drained at least 1 hour before the earliest arrival in the trajectory window.
Own the Call: you decide on the intake, not Ironbark, and Ironbark's pressure does not change that.
Critical Customers: call the dialysis center, the medical center and the nursing homes directly before any public notice.
Reopen on Evidence: reopen only on the recommendations of the Environmental Unit and the state drinking water program, with plant tests showing no sheen, no hydrocarbons and no taste or odor problem.

phases.title: Pressure Drop at 214.3
phases.goal: Tests whether the Control Center recognizes an unconfirmed leak signal, shuts down and closes the block valves on time, and whether the person in charge reports to the National Response Center within 15 minutes without waiting for the Qualified Individual, as SNIMTA 2 requires.
beats: (05:52) Pipeline Control Center in Tulsa: SCADA shows a 46 psi pressure drop in 2 minutes at the Prairie Bend segment and computational pipeline monitoring flags a 1.8 percent flow imbalance. Nothing confirms it. Shift supervisor Nadia Kowalczyk must start the 10-minute rule-out clock from SNIMTA 2.

Noise item (05:56): a routine tank-gauge maintenance ticket and a nuisance alarm from Wabash Junction Terminal come in on the same console. Both are unrelated to milepost 214.3 and pull attention away from the leak signal.

(06:02) The leak cannot be ruled out. A technical note says the monitoring did not isolate the leak location, so the supervisor still has no confirmed loss. Shutdown follows at 06:04, and Mill Ridge Station (MP 213.1) and Sandhill Valve (MP 215.6) are confirmed closed by 06:09. Test whether the NRC report goes in by 06:17 with the person in charge calling, and whether the QI Teresa Holloway call is made and logged with the time and the speaker.

(06:20) The first SCADA volume balance gives 2,700 to 3,500 barrels of medium sour crude, with 3,100 barrels as the planning figure. It is an estimate, not a worst case discharge. The supervisor must report it as a range with its basis and must not guess the cause.

(06:35–06:45) SimCell: a fisherman's 911 call reaches Prairie Bend County emergency management, which calls Ironbark asking about 'oil in the ditch by the river.' At about 06:40 crude enters the Kansas River through the drainage ditch, so the county hears of the spill before Ironbark calls them.

phases.title: Oil on the Kaw
phases.goal: Tests whether the QI activates Prairie Spill Response Cooperative and makes the state, intake-operator and county notifications in the plan's order, and whether the Environmental Unit produces the first trajectory with arrival windows and the model run time, all while a red herring and the press split the team's attention.
beats: (06:50) Duty Manager Alicia Brandt of Prairie Spill Response Cooperative accepts activation. The first boom can be at the nearest ramp about 3.5 hours after notification. There are 9,500 feet of river boom spread across the depots and only a few boats. Nobody in the room believes the estimate holds at a 2-knot current.

(07:00) SimCell red herring: a Control Center technician suggests the pressure drop was a SCADA communications or instrument fault and proposes delaying the KDHE and intake calls until there is visual confirmation. The team splits, which tests whether the SNIMTA 2 30-minute notifications to KDHE, the Kansas Division of Emergency Management, the Prairie Bend Rural Water District (mile 11) and the Sterling Bluff Water Department (mile 34) go ahead anyway.

Visual confirmation for the room (07:10): a county deputy's photo and drone still show black crude and sheen moving past the Mill Ridge boat ramp. The Environmental Unit's first trajectory gives arrival windows for the ramp, the plover sandbars at miles 6 to 9, the mile 11 intake, Cottonwood Slough (mile 22) and the mile 34 intake, stamped with the model run time.

(07:20) Notification friction: the Environmental Unit's call to the rural water district reaches only the district's general office line, and the Sterling Bluff call goes to a front-desk voicemail. Under SNIMTA 2 neither call counts until an operator is reached. The log must show who was reached, when, and what was said.

(07:30) SimCell: a local reporter's social post says '100,000 gallons in the river,' and residents start calling the Ironbark line. The PIO must answer with the single barrel range and its SCADA basis, without mixing units and without confirming a cause.

phases.title: Close the Intake?
phases.goal: Tests the one decision point: whether the Sterling Bluff Director decides to stop drawing river water and run on about 34 hours of storage early, or to keep the intake open longer to protect supply. Also tests whether Unified Command puts the limited angled boom where it matters, consults USFWS before working near the nests, and sends any countermeasure request to the FOSC.
beats: (07:50) Unified Command forms at Mill Ridge Station with IC Gordon Iwata, the EPA Region 7 FOSC and the KDHE state OSC (SimCell). The updated trajectory, with its model run time, puts oil at the mile 11 intake in a window around 10:50 to 12:00 (about 4.8 hours after river entry) and at the mile 34 Sterling Bluff intake in a window around 20:45 to 22:30 (about 14.8 hours).

DECISION POINT (08:05): Director Odell Prescott must decide whether to close the Sterling Bluff intake now and run on storage, wells and the connection, or keep drawing river water until closer to the window. Closing early cuts the 34 hours of supply short and strains service to the dialysis center, the Sterling Bluff Medical Center and the two nursing homes. Closing late risks oil in the plant, because Sterling Bluff plan 4 requires the gate closed and the line drained at least 1 hour before the earliest arrival. Ironbark may advise but must not decide.

(08:15) Partner friction: the SimCell rural water district manager, who has no wells and only storage, says the district will close the mile 11 intake and asks to buy water from Sterling Bluff through the interconnect. That would draw down Sterling Bluff's storage just as the Director decides. Sterling Bluff must also call its vulnerable customers directly.

(08:25) Boom allocation: the cooperative proposes deflection boom at mile 9.5 and exclusion boom at the mile 11 intake, plus three deflection stations at miles 28, 31 and 33 and exclusion boom at Sterling Bluff and Cottonwood Slough, all from 9,500 feet and a few boats. Boom must be angled at about 15 degrees, not set square. A crew wants to stake boom on the plover sandbars at miles 6 to 9, and USFWS (SimCell) must be consulted first. A field lead suggests burning the pooled oil in the ditch, which must go to the FOSC because burning is not preauthorized on this river.

Media pressure (08:35): a regional TV reporter goes live at 09:00 and asks Ironbark whether Sterling Bluff's water is safe to drink. The JIC must clear a message with the Ironbark, EPA, KDHE and county PIOs that gives the barrel range, leaves intake status and drinking-water statements to the utilities and the state, and announces the claims line before 09:00.

phases.title: Reopening the River
phases.goal: Tests verification before trusting recovery: whether boom failures are caught and reset, whether the intake reopens only on the Sterling Bluff plan 4 criteria, and whether the remaining notifications, the wildlife report and the after-action note are completed.
beats: Time jump to Wednesday 9 June, 08:45 (exercise 3:00): the leading edge passed mile 34 overnight. The deflection stations recovered oil into the bank pockets, and the questions on the table are what comes back first (Mill Ridge ramp and fishing access by KDWP decision, then the rural water district intake, then Sterling Bluff) and who decides.

Hurdle (08:55): at the 2-hour boom check, the stakes at the mile 31 deflection station have pulled out and a fresh sheen is heading for the Sterling Bluff exclusion boom. Oil trapped in Cottonwood Slough is also re-mobilizing on the morning flow. The replacement boom sections are a depot away, several hours out, and the trajectory must be re-run with a new model run time.

Verification (09:05): Director Odell Prescott is pressed to reopen because storage is down to about 12 hours. The plant's first sample shows hydrocarbons just above the action level. Under Sterling Bluff plan 4, reopening needs the Environmental Unit recommendation, the state drinking water program's concurrence and clean plant results, and the JIC still must not call the water 'safe.'

(09:15) The Environmental Unit's wildlife status report for the USFWS and KDWP trustees gives counts as oiled live, oiled dead, hazed, in rehabilitation and released. SCAT teams report oiling categories by segment, with manual removal only on the nesting sandbars. The volume estimate is updated as a barrel range with its basis.

(07:30–07:45) Final notifications are logged: a PHMSA follow-up and an update to the NRC report (SimCell). The team checks the notification log against SNIMTA 2 and drafts the after-action note covering notification timing, the general-line problem and the intake decision. ENDEX.

msel.from: Prairie Spill Response Cooperative Topeka depot lead (SimCell)
msel.event: Radio Call (Topeka depot lead to the cooperative duty desk, relayed to the Ironbark QI line, 06:50): "Duty desk, Topeka depot. We got the activation page at 06:48. One crew is loading the trailer now: 3,000 feet of 18-inch river boom, two skimmers, two shallow-draft boats. If we're rolling by 07:30, I can have the first boom at the Mill Ridge ramp around 10:20. Wichita says they have 2,500 feet ready but no driver until 08:00. Kansas City has 4,000 feet and six boats, but the subcontractor dispatcher says he can't put crews on those boats for at least four hours unless somebody calls Tier 2 now. Also, your Ironbark ops chief phoned me directly and wants the boom strung straight across the river at the ramp. At 2 knots that boom just passes oil underneath it. It refuses square-across boom and plans angled deflection at about 15 degrees toward bank recovery pockets, per the Cooperative plan 4. QI confirms the funding commitment and records the activation in the notification log. QI sends boom-site priorities through Unified Command and the ICS 202 so the first caller doesn't decide them, and accepts that the ramp is already lost while the mile 9.5 deflection site and the mile 11 intake come first.

msel.event: Face-to-Face (SCADA technician at the PLC-2 console, 07:00): "Nadia Kowalczyk, look at this. The RTU at Mill Ridge Station logged two comm retries at 05:51:58, just before the pressure drop. I think we chased a comms or transmitter fault. The Prairie Bend Rural Water District manager has called back. Ironbark's public line has 31 calls in queue, and Prairie 6 News is now camped at the Mill Ridge gate. "We're Unified Command as of now. Ironbark is the responsible party. I want draft ICS 202 objectives and an ICS 232 in 30 minutes. NOAA's support coordinator just pushed an update to your Environmental Unit; walk us through it." On screen: Trajectory Product TRJ-02, model run 07:45 CDT, the NOAA Scientific Support Coordinator (SimCell). Basis: river entry ~06:40, leading edge seen by county drone at RM 2.4 at 07:40, USGS gauge 8,500 cfs, surface velocity 2.3 mph, ±15% band (narrowed from ±20% by the observation). msel.from: Sterling Bluff Water Department plant superintendent (SimCell)
msel.event: Phone Call (plant superintendent to Director Odell Prescott, 08:05, speaker on): "Boss, here's where we are. Storage is 10.6 million gallons, 96 percent full. Wells are making 0.9 MGD and demand is tracking 8.4 this morning. Raw water at 08:00 is clean: no sheen, no odor, TOC 2.1. If you shut the gate now we have about 34 hours on storage and wells. That runs out around 18:00 tomorrow, and nobody can tell me when this oil finishes passing. If we keep drawing, the earliest arrival is 20:45 tonight. The gate takes 20 minutes and the line takes 40 to drain, so I'd have to start closing by 18:45 at the latest, and I'd rather give that a margin. The dialysis center runs its big shift at 13:00. Ironbark's liaison is in the lobby and says 'Ironbark recommends you close now, we'll cover bottled water.' What do you want me to do?" An email from Ironbark Liaison <liaison@ironbarkpipeline.example> arrives at the same time: "SUBJECT: Recommendation – Sterling Bluff intake. Ironbark respectfully recommends immediate closure."
msel.expectedAction: DECISION POINT: The SBWD Director must decide, himself, whether to close the intake now and run on storage, wells and the connection, or keep drawing river water and set a hard closure time. A late closure must be complete by 19:45 at the latest, so it starts no later than 18:45 under the plan's decision-timing rule. He weighs the hours of supply, a 25% conservation request and the risk to critical-care customers, and records the decision and its basis. The ENVL gives the window and its uncertainty but no decision. The QI makes sure Ironbark only advises and offers to pay for supply.

msel.event: Time Jump: The exercise moves forward one day. It is now 08:45 CDT, Wednesday 9 June 2027, about 27 hours after the line was shut in. hotwash.methodDescription: Ask the room for three things that went well and three things that broke or failed during the exercise. Go around the room one team at a time (Control Center, Ironbark command, spill co-op, agencies, utilities, PIOs). Write every answer on the whiteboard in two columns so the room can see the patterns before the facilitator moves to the discussion questions.

questions.text: At I-02 the CPM analyst told you at 06:02 that a leak could not be ruled out, but the location estimate covered MP 209 to MP 219 and nobody in the field could see anything. When did you treat that moment as a reportable release and start the 15-minute clock for the National Response Center report? Did the shutdown decision wait for a confirmation that SCADA could never give you? What would have let the console and the QI decide faster?

At I-09 the first calls to the Prairie Bend RWD and Sterling Bluff WD reached a clerk and a front-desk voicemail, not an operator. One call went to a clerk who left a note on a desk, and the other went to a front-desk voicemail. The Sterling Bluff superintendent learned about the oil from a county page. Who did you actually reach? Why did the log count a voicemail as a notification? What direct contacts for the intake operators should be in the plan before the next event?

At I-13 and I-13b both utilities made closure decisions from your trajectory. The RWD closed at 09:00 against a 10:50 earliest arrival. Sterling Bluff had a latest gate start of 18:45 against a 20:45 arrival. How old was the model run each of them was using, and did they know when it would be updated? Did your ICS 232 priorities match the order the oil would reach the plover sandbars, the mile 11 intake, Cottonwood Slough and Sterling Bluff?

At I-13 the Ironbark liaison stood in the Sterling Bluff lobby and emailed that Ironbark 'recommends immediate closure.' Then at I-13b the RWD asked to reverse the interconnect, although the Sterling Bluff storage figure assumed water flowing the other way, and asked Ironbark to put payment in writing. Who in the room thought they owned the intake decisions? Did anyone notice the interconnect conflict before the two utilities committed to it? Who took on the call to the Prairie Haven nursing home, and who should make it?

At I-04b and I-10 the public saw '10,000 barrels' and '100,000 gallons' before they heard anything from you. A reporter wanted gallons and a cause on camera by 7:40, and a mother called about her newborn's tap water. What was the first cleared JIC message you released, and when did it go out? Did it give one barrel range with its SCADA basis, without guessing at a cause? Did it send drinking-water questions to the utilities and KDHE, and did it open a claims line? Which of the four PIO clearances slowed you down most?

simcellScripts.trigger: The Control Center Shift Supervisor (or anyone at Ironbark) calls the NRC to report the release, or the NRC callback at I-03 or I-20 is answered.
hardQuestions: "Are you the person in charge of the facility? Give me your name, the time you shut in, and the quantity. A range is fine, but tell me what it's based on, and use barrels or gallons, not both."

"The cause field says unknown. Was this third-party damage or corrosion? EPA Region 7 and KDHE are asking. You're telling me you don't know? Then I'm writing 'unknown', and don't phone me a guess later."
"Has oil reached the water? Which water body, and what river mile? I need a latitude and longitude or a milepost, not 'near the ramp.'"
"Just so you know, I'm not sending anyone and I'm not approving anything. If you need boom, call your OSRO. Have you called them?"
concessions: Gives the report number 1398274 and the time of the report once the person in charge has reported quantity, location, the material and that oil is on the water.
Accepts a range with its basis (for example '2,700–3,500 bbl, SCADA volume balance, unverified') and confirms the NRC will relay it to EPA Region 7 and KDHE.
Records the update for the Wednesday follow-up (I-20) only if the revised range VB-0621 comes with its basis and the cause stays 'unknown' rather than a guess.

simcellScripts.rolePlayed: Prairie Bend Rural Water District Manager Carl Dunning (the utility, which depends on the Sterling Bluff interconnect and serves Prairie Haven nursing home)
simcellScripts.trigger: An Ironbark player or the Sterling Bluff Director reaches the manager directly at (785) 555-0173. A call to the general office line 555-0147 reaches only the clerk (I-09). The manager calls back at I-13b.
hardQuestions: "You left a note with my clerk at 07:14 and your log says I was notified? I'm the operator. When did oil hit the river, and what's my arrival window, with your model run time? Not 'a few hours.'"

"I've got no wells and 1.1 million gallons. If I close at 09:00 I'm buying 0.5 MGD from Sterling Bluff through an interconnect that's set up to flow the other way. Who's paying for that, and where's it in writing? Your liaison said 'we'll cover it.' That isn't a document."
"Prairie Haven nursing home is already calling me. Is Ironbark's JIC going to tell my customers anything about my water? Because that's my call and KDHE's, not yours."
"Sterling Bluff, which comes first on the interconnect today, my 6,200 or your dialysis center? Sterling Bluff plan 6 says we agree on each call. So let's agree."
concessions: Gives a firm intake closure time (09:00) and the storage figure, but only after a named Ironbark person gives him the trajectory product with arrival windows and model run time and logs him as reached.
Agrees to a joint interconnect priority with the Sterling Bluff Director once the Director commits a flow rate and start time.
Sends the district's own customer notice through the JIC only after Ironbark puts its cost commitment in writing (signed by the QI) and agrees the district alone speaks about its water status.

simcellScripts.rolePlayed: EPA Region 7 Federal On-Scene Coordinator (seated with the KDHE state On-Scene Coordinator at Mill Ridge Station)
simcellScripts.trigger: The QI confirms and joins Unified Command (I-12), or anyone asks for approval of in-situ burning, dispersant, or a chemical sorbent such as the BioSheen Eraser (I-14, I-19b).
hardQuestions: "Draft ICS 202 objectives and an ICS 232 in 30 minutes. What's your number one resource at risk and why? Plovers, the mile 11 intake or Sterling Bluff? Show me the ranking, not a list."

"Your field lead wants to light off the ditch pool. Burning isn't preauthorized on this river. Give me a written request: the volume, how weathered the oil is, wind direction, distance to the road and the homes, the smoke plume toward people, and who's monitoring. Without that, the answer is no."
"Is the Sterling Bluff operator holding TRJ-02, or did someone leave a voicemail at the front desk? KDHE's drinking water bureau wants the name and the time."
"Someone in your shop is saying 'the water is safe.' Who cleared that? Ironbark doesn't close or open intakes and doesn't certify drinking water."
concessions: Signs the ICS 202 objectives once they include public health and water intakes, the ranked sensitive areas, angled deflection boom and wildlife under USFWS and KDWP direction.

Decides on a countermeasure only after a complete written request, and gives the decision with its conditions and the time. With no RRT preauthorization, the default is denial or 'pending RRT concurrence.'
Has the KDHE OSC confirm drinking-water coordination once the EU shows a named operator-level contact and time for both utilities.

simcellScripts.rolePlayed: US Fish and Wildlife Service, Kansas field office biologist
simcellScripts.trigger: A crew is sent toward the plover sandbars at miles 6–9 (I-14 Crew 3, I-19 skid steer), the Environmental Unit calls as a trustee, or the wildlife report goes out (I-19).
hardQuestions: "Who authorized a crew on the bars at mile 7? There are active piping plover nests on at least two of them. Nobody sets a stake or drives a skid steer there until I've talked to your Environmental Unit. Who is that, by name?"
"Square boom staked across the bar heads? At 2 knots it won't hold oil, and you'll trample nests setting it. Show me a deflection plan that keeps people off the bars."
"Your wildlife report counts the oiled plover adult under both live and rehab. Which is it? I need oiled live, oiled dead, hazed, in rehab and released, each counted once."
"Who did the hazing? If it wasn't authorized personnel under our direction, I need to know now."
concessions: Approves manual removal only on bars 2 and 3, with a USFWS escort, once the EU asks for consultation before the work and names a crew lead.
Accepts a corrected wildlife status report (no double count) with times and locations, and confirms it is going to KDWP.
Agrees to deflection boom placed downstream of the bars (for example mile 9.5) in place of work on the bars themselves.

simcellScripts.rolePlayed: Prairie 6 News reporter (@DanaReportsP6), assignment desk via pio@ironbarkpipeline.example
simcellScripts.trigger: The PIO answers the reporter's email or call (I-04b, I-10, I-15), or anyone at Ironbark speaks to the press at the Mill Ridge gate.
hardQuestions: "I'm live at 9:00. Yes or no, on camera: is Sterling Bluff's tap water safe to drink?"
"My sources say 100,000 gallons. If you won't give me a number, that one stands. What's yours, in gallons, right now?"
"Corrosion or someone hit the line? You've had three hours. Ironbark doesn't know why its own pipe broke?"
"The bait shop owners say nobody's told them who pays. Is there a claims number, or do they call the station?"
concessions: Corrects the on-air figure to the JIC's single range (for example 2,700–3,500 bbl, an estimate from the SCADA volume balance) if a spokesperson gives it, with its basis, before the deadline.
Runs the claims line 555-0131 and the utilities' own water-status contacts if the PIO gives them in a cleared statement.
Takes 'the cause is under investigation' with no follow-up rumor only if the PIO also gives a firm time for the next briefing and keeps it.

assumptions: The exercise is conducted in a no-fault learning environment. The aim is to test the Ironbark Response Plan, the SNIMTA first-hour actions and the partner plans, not to evaluate individual players.
The scenario is plausible, and events occur as they are presented. Players accept the river flow, the volume figures and the arrival times as given, even where they differ from local experience.

Players respond in accordance with existing plans, policies and procedures, including the Ironbark Response Plan, the SNIMTA first-hour table and the Prairie Spill Response Cooperative plan. Where a plan is silent, players describe what they would do and who would decide it.
The cause of the release is not known to players and is not part of the exercise. Players work with the information they have at the start of each module and the injects they receive during it.

Decisions that belong to agencies or utilities not in the room are simulated. These include the FOSC's countermeasure approvals, USFWS consultation, KDHE concurrence and intake closures by the districts. Players state the decision they would request and who they would request it from.
The release is the 3,100-barrel planning-range scenario, not the 8,400-barrel worst case discharge. All volumes are discussed in barrels.
artificialities: Time is compressed. The exercise runs four one-hour modules, and Module 4 jumps forward to 08:45 CDT on Wednesday 9 June 2027. Events between modules are summarized on the facilitator's time-jump cards.

A SimCell plays everyone outside the room. This includes the National Response Center, EPA Region 7 and the KDHE On-Scene Coordinators, PHMSA, USFWS, KDWP, Prairie Bend County Emergency Management and the sheriff, the Prairie Bend Rural Water District, the Sterling Bluff plant superintendent and city officials, the Prairie Spill field crews, the media, residents and vendors.

SCADA, computational pipeline monitoring, the block valves, the trajectory model, the NRC reporting line and the 555- public and claims lines are named as in the plans but are not operated or dialed. Their outputs arrive as printed or on-screen injects.

Injects are delivered on paper or on screen: alarms, phone calls, emails, social media posts, ICS 213 messages and status boards. Players respond by discussion, not by placing real calls or posting real messages.
No boom, boats, crews or samples are deployed. Equipment arrival times and field conditions are as stated in the injects.

modules.narrativeMd:
**Module 1: Pressure Drop at 214.3** (exercise time 0:00–1:00; scenario 05:45–06:45 CDT, Tuesday 8 June 2027)

It is 05:45 Central Daylight Time. It is clear and warm with a light south wind, and sunrise has just passed. The Kansas River is running about 8,500 cfs with a surface velocity near 2.3 mph (2 knots). In the Ironbark Pipeline Control Center in Tulsa, shift supervisor Nadia Kowalczyk has finished the day shift handover.

The Prairie Line is moving about 31,000 barrels a day of medium sour crude toward Wabash Junction Terminal. Pressure at the milepost 214.3 Kansas River crossing is about 880 psi. Mill Ridge Station (MP 213.1) and Sandhill Valve (MP 215.6) both show OPEN and remotely available. SCADA and computational pipeline monitoring are green, and all status is normal.

Shutting down and closing the block valves before the cause or the location is known
Making the person in charge's NRC report within 15 minutes without waiting for the Qualified Individual
Keeping routine terminal and maintenance traffic from pulling attention away from the console
Logging each notification with time, caller and content from the first call

**Module 2: Oil on the Kaw** (exercise time 1:00–2:00; scenario 06:45–07:45 CDT, Tuesday 8 June 2027)

It is 06:45 CDT. At 05:52 a pressure drop and a flow imbalance were flagged at the 214.3 crossing. At 06:02 the CPM analyst could neither rule out a leak nor locate one. The Prairie Line was shut in at 06:04, and Mill Ridge Station and Sandhill Valve were closed by 06:09. A National Response Center report (1398274) is on file. The NRC has called back asking for an updated quantity and for something in the cause field. The SCADA volume balance (VB-0620) reads 2,700–3,500 barrels of medium sour crude: a planning figure of 3,100 barrels, UNVERIFIED.

At 06:37 Prairie Bend County Emergency Management called to say its 911 had taken a fisherman's report of black, rotten-egg-smelling oil in a ditch at the Mill Ridge boat ramp. The county said nobody from Ironbark had called them, and it put an unconfirmed page on its partner page. By 06:41 the fisherman reported a brown sheen moving downstream fast. A Facebook post claiming '10,000 barrels' and 'poisoned' tap water is spreading with a ditch video. Prairie 6 News wants confirmation for a 07:00 live shot. The IMT is being called out at Level 2, with Gordon Iwata as Incident Commander and Cole Whitfield leading the Environmental Unit. Nobody has filled in the notification log past the NRC call.

**Module 3: Close the Intake?** (exercise time 2:00–3:00; scenario 07:45–08:45 CDT, Tuesday 8 June 2027)

It is 07:45 CDT. The leading edge of the slick is about 2.5 river miles below the crossing and moving at roughly 2.3 miles an hour. The first trajectory (TRJ-01, run 07:05) shows the plover sandbars at 08:50–11:25, the mile 11 Prairie Bend RWD intake at 10:40–12:25, Cottonwood Slough at 14:40–18:10 and the mile 34 Sterling Bluff intake between 19:00 Tuesday and 00:25 Wednesday. KDWP has closed the Mill Ridge boat ramp and the Kaw Valley Fishing Access. The volume is still 2,700–3,500 barrels (planning figure 3,100 barrels, SCADA volume balance, UNVERIFIED).

Prairie Spill has 9,500 feet of 18-inch river boom across three depots and four crewed shallow-draft boats. The first boom is due at the ramp around 10:20. The Ironbark IMT is at Level 2, with the command post setting up at Mill Ridge Station, and the EPA Region 7 FOSC and the KDHE state OSC are 10 minutes out. Sterling Bluff began hourly raw-water sampling at 07:30, and the rural water district manager has called back. A Prairie 6 News reporter has posted '100,000 gallons' and asked about corrosion, and the crew is now at the Mill Ridge gate. Ironbark's public line has 31 calls waiting.

modules.narrativeMd:
**Module 4: Reopening the River** (exercise time 3:00–4:00; scenario 08:45–09:45 CDT, Wednesday 9 June 2027)

It is 08:45 CDT on Wednesday 9 June 2027, about 27 hours after the line was shut in. The leading edge passed mile 34 overnight, inside the TRJ-02 window. The Prairie Line is still shut in, with Mill Ridge Station and Sandhill Valve closed. Overnight the deflection stations at miles 9.5, 28, 31 and 33 pushed oil into bank recovery pockets. Recovered oily liquid fills six 500-barrel portable tanks at Mill Ridge staging; this is an oil-and-water mixture, not an oil volume. The river is still about 8,500 cfs at about 2 knots.

Overnight reports put the leading edge past all intakes. The Prairie Bend RWD has been buying water through the interconnect since yesterday afternoon. Sterling Bluff has run on storage and wells since its gate closed yesterday. The JIC queue is down to 19 calls, and the claims line (555-0131) is ringing steadily.

Keeping the trajectory current as conditions change after the leading edge has passed
Reopening intakes only on the utility's criteria, with KDHE concurrence, not on 'the river looks clean'

Completing the NRC and PHMSA updates, correcting the notification log and writing the after-action note with one barrel range
